bib.title: CodeSearchNet Challenge: Evaluating the State of Semantic Code Search

question: How can progress on semantic code search (natural-language query to code) be measured, and how well do simple neural and keyword baselines do?
contributions: CodeSearchNet Corpus of about 6 million functions in six languages, about 2 million with documentation
CodeSearchNet Challenge: 99 natural language queries with about 4k expert relevance annotations
Baseline models (NBoW, 1D-CNN, biRNN, self-attention, ElasticSearch) and a leaderboard

method.summary: Scraped open-source GitHub functions paired with first-paragraph documentation as a proxy training set; built 99 queries from Bing and StaQC with expert relevance labels for top-10 candidates per query and language; trained joint code/query embedding baselines with a softmax contrastive loss and compared with ElasticSearch.
method.task: semantic code search (retrieval of functions for natural language queries)

datasets.name: CodeSearchNet Corpus
datasets.source: open-source non-fork GitHub repos via libraries.io, sorted by stars and forks, with redistributable licences
datasets.preprocessing: TreeSitter tokenisation; docs truncated to first paragraph; pairs with doc under 3 tokens dropped; functions under 3 lines dropped; names containing 'test', constructors and standard extension methods dropped; near-duplicates removed

datasets.name: CodeSearchNet Challenge
datasets.source: Bing queries with high click-through to code plus StaQC intent rewrites; volunteer expert annotators; candidates from ensemble of all neural models and ElasticSearch (top 10 per query and language)
datasets.preprocessing: queries that are exact technical keywords removed

models.name: NBoW
models.tokenizer: code identifiers split into subtokens; natural language BPE

models.name: ElasticSearch
models.architecture: keyword search, default parameters and tokenizer, two fields: function name in subtokens and entire function text

training.objective: minimise -1/N sum_i log( exp(Ec(ci)^T Eq(di)) / sum_j exp(Ec(cj)^T Eq(di)) ), other snippets in batch as distractors

other.pooling: mean/max-pooling and attention-like weighted sum implemented; which used per model not stated
other.alternatives: cosine similarity and max-margin objectives tried, no significant change on validation

inference.samples: single run per model; seeds not stated
inference.retrieval: all functions in the corpus (including undocumented) indexed with Annoy approximate nearest neighbours; query embedded and nearest code returned

parameters.annoy_trees: not stated; paper says a small number of trees made baselines underperform

metrics.name: MRR
metrics.definition: mean reciprocal rank of the correct snippet for a docstring query among 999 distractors, on corpus test split

metrics.name: NDCG Within
metrics.definition: NDCG over the subset of functions with human annotations

metrics.name: NDCG All
metrics.definition: NDCG over the whole CodeSearchNet Corpus; unannotated relevant results count against a tool

eval.protocol: Inter-annotator agreement on 891 query-code pairs with more than one annotation: Cohen kappa 0.47. Distractor set of 999 fixed per test pair. No seeds or significance tests.

limits: Training data is documentation-derived, which differs from real queries; authors say it is a noisy proxy and not a good match for code search.
Annotations are few (about 4k), mostly one per pair, skewed by language (Python 2 089 of 4 026), from volunteers; kappa only 0.47.
Candidates to annotate were chosen by the baselines themselves, so NDCG Within favours them and NDCG All penalises unannotated relevant results.
Baselines report no hyperparameters, seeds or variance; pooling choice per model unstated.
A later indexing bug (Annoy trees) was found by an outside participant and affected results; the v3 numbers are the corrected ones.
English queries only; whole functions only, not code chunks.
